snippet.text: A dichroic beamsplitter divides the incident collimated beam, reflecting the VIS wavelengths portion of the bandpass (λ < 950 nm) and transmitting NIR wavelengths (λ > 950 nm). It is fabricated from fused silica, 160 x 160 x 35 mm, with the dichroic coating applied to the incident surface. snippet.text:
Multispectral imaging like color imaging in visible spectrum provides more important information in spectral domain than gray scale imaging [1,2]. Color filters in visible spectrum utilize organic dyes to create colors by absorbing some portion of spectrum in incident light [3]. It is unfortunately more challenging to realize multispectral filters in infrared, in particular mid-infrared (MIR), in the same way [4]. Midinfrared spectral analysis provides a highly sensitive and selective method for chemical detection, which may find a wide range of applications in gas sensing, noninvasive disease diagnosis, security monitoring and others [5][6][7]. Multilayer Bragg filters, which rely on the layer thicknesses to create phase shift for spectral modification, are often employed as multispectral filters in MIR due to their high spectral performance. However, it is extremely complex to integrate Bragg multispectral films on imaging chip by standard complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) processes. For this reason, multilayered Bragg filters are used separately with one filter for one imaging chip, resulting in a complicated bulky system [8]. 

Plasmonic spectral filters utilize the surface plasmon polaritons in metal surfaces to realize spectral filtering [9,10]. The filtering spectrum can be adjusted by tuning the periodicity and size of the nanostructures in the metal thin film [11][12][13]. A large array of spectral filters can be readily integrated onto the image pixels by CMOS fabrication processes [14]. However, plasmonic filters made of periodic regular shapes of apertures in metal films often have a Gaussian passband and relatively low transmission peak and bad crosstalk [15][16][17], which are not desirable for practical applications. Plasmonic nanostructured filters by inverse design possess a high degree of freedom to generate random structures, corresponding to a desired spectra with quasi-square shape, high transmission, large full width at half maximum (FWHM) and low crosstalk.

We show example reflectivity curves of the planned dichroic coatings at 15 • incidence angle in Figure 16. We chose this style of coating as they are low stress evaporative coatings with reasonable repeatability and achievable 1% physical thickness uniformity across the entire aperture.

The retardance of the reflected beam at 15 • incidence angle is shown in the right hand graphic of Figure 17. The thickest coating is C-BS-950 with 96 layers and an 8.8 µm physical thickness. There are strong spectral variations expected in retardance curves for dichroics with tens of layers. The theoretical retardance derivative has several bandpasses with gradients of 10 • per nanometer wavelength with a few specific narrow features up to magnitudes of 100 • retardance per nm wavelength. We show in this section that these rapid swings in retardance are observable and can also be mitigated by design. Similarly, these narrow spectral features in dichroic coatings are also coincident with significant diattenuation as well as strong changes in transmission. snippet.text: Multispectral imaging technology is regarded as a non-destructive inspection method for building materials. It examines the color fingerprints of reflected light to determine the degree of concrete hardness, the level of moisture inside, and the strength of the structure. It detects light beyond the range of the human eye, uncovering problems that are invisible through ordinary methods, such as the amount of debris mixed in the cement and the moisture content of the raw materials. By combining visible light, near-infrared, and short-wave infrared, it provides a more comprehensive material inspection report than RGB photos. The technology captures the minute differences in material molecules and can distinguish identical materials, providing more accurate classification, greater recycling, and less waste. The old RGB system has only three color channels and cannot detect these subtle differences. Multispectral imaging has broken through this barrier and provided a reliable solution for the identification of complex materials in civil and environmental engineering.

The samples were illuminated with different light sources ranging from IR to UV A (365 nm). The images capture distinct differences in visible-induced luminescence and reflectance amongst the samples. Photoshop was used to process "raw" .dng images. Color was corrected using standard gray swatches, and "spectralon," a material with high diffuse reflectance, was used to compare relative reflectance along with other color, scale, and UV-indicating fiducials.

The dichroic suite is thus 465, 555, 643, 680 and 950. We also show in Table 6, the appropriate anti-reflection coating intended for the back surface. This will either be WBBAR1 described above or the related coating WBBAR2.

We are in the process of verifying the coating performance, repeatability, spatial uniformity, stress, wavefront error, etc so we list TBD in Table 6. We also list three dichroic samples used in early evaluation and design from Infinite Optics that we label Dich. A, B and C.

We show example reflectivity curves of the planned dichroic coatings at 15 • incidence angle in Figure 16. The designs have fairly sharp transitions with most coatings switching from 80% reflective to 80% transmissive in less than 10 nm wavelength. We chose this style of coating as they are low stress evaporative coatings with reasonable repeatability and achievable 1% physical thickness uniformity across the entire aperture.

The retardance of the reflected beam at 15 • incidence angle is shown in the right hand graphic of Figure 17. The thickest coating is C-BS-950 with 96 layers and an 8.8 µm physical thickness. There are strong spectral variations expected in retardance curves for dichroics with tens of layers. The theoretical retardance derivative has several bandpasses with gradients of 10 • per nanometer wavelength with a few specific narrow features up to magnitudes of 100 • retardance per nm wavelength. We show in this section that these rapid swings in retardance are observable and can also be mitigated by design. Similarly, these narrow spectral features in dichroic coatings are also coincident with significant diattenuation as well as strong changes in transmission. All of these narrow spectral features of dichroics have impact for DKIST calibration as we can possibly anticipate strong spectral changes across the ∼nm instrument bandpasses in the modulation matrix through retardance and diattenuation, in addition to substantial throughput changes. results.title: Intelligent Sorting and Quality Control of Construction Site Materials by Fusing Machine Vision and Multi-spectral Imaging
results.snippet_text: Multispectral imaging technology is regarded as a non-destructive inspection method for building materials. It examines the color fingerprints of reflected light to determine the degree of concrete hardness, the level of moisture inside, and the strength of the structure. It detects light beyond the range of the human eye, uncovering problems that are invisible through ordinary methods, such as the amount of debris mixed in the cement and the moisture content of the raw materials. By combining visible light, near-infrared, and short-wave infrared, it provides a more comprehensive material inspection report than RGB photos. The technology captures the minute differences in material molecules and can distinguish identical materials, providing more accurate classification, greater recycling, and less waste. The old RGB system has only three color channels and cannot detect these subtle differences. Multispectral imaging has broken through this barrier and provided a reliable solution for the identification of complex materials in civil and environmental engineering.
